target.title: Voice Activity Detection for Ultrasound-based Silent Speech Interfaces using Convolutional Neural Networks

read.pdf: Tables 1–7 and figure references/captions for Figs. 1–4 reviewed in text.txt; PDF not supplied for visual inspection.

entries.text: The paper trains a CNN to separate speech and silence directly from ultrasound tongue images and compares the SSI system with and without VAD.
entries.condition: TaL1 ultrasound tongue images; speech/silence labels are derived from synchronized speech using a conventional VAD.
entries.quote:
Then we implement a CNN to separate
silence and speech frames based on the ultrasound tongue images, so we basically
create a VAD algorithm that works with ultrasound images.

entries.text: The TAL corpus contains recordings from 81 native English speakers.
entries.condition: Overall TAL corpus, not the subset used in the experiments.

entries.text: The TAL ultrasound dataset used in the SSI and classifier experiments is TaL1 from one male native speaker.
entries.condition: SSI and classifier experiments; the separate speech-only analysis-synthesis experiment's dataset is not identified.
entries.quote:
we used just the TaL1 subset which contains recordings from one male native
speaker.

entries.text: The speaker's files were partitioned into training, test, and validation sets of 1015, 24, and 50 files.
entries.condition: Files from the single TaL1 speaker; the paper does not report a session-level partition.
entries.quote:
We partitioned his ﬁles into training, testing and validation sets using
1015, 24 and 50 ﬁles, respectively.

entries.text: Ultrasound images are min-max normalized to [-1,1] and resized to 64×128 by bicubic interpolation.
entries.condition: Ultrasound preprocessing; SSI mel-spectrogram target features are standardized separately.

entries.text: The SSI input ultrasound tongue images are recorded at 82 frames per second.
entries.condition: UTI acquisition rate for the SSI framework.
entries.quote:
The in-
put of the system is a sequence of ultrasound tongue images (UTI) that were
recorded at a rate of 82 frames per second.

entries.text: The SSI network predicts 80 mel-spectrogram coefficients, which WaveGlow converts to speech.
entries.condition: UTI-to-spectral regression followed by WaveGlow neural vocoding.
entries.quote:
These 80 mel-spectrogram coeﬃcients served as the training target
values for the SSI network.

entries.text: SSI regressors are 3D-CNN and 3D-CNN+BiLSTM sequence models trained to minimize spectral MSE.
entries.condition: Sequence of adjacent UTI frames as input; 80-dimensional mel-spectral vector as output; Table 1 gives layer structures.

entries.text: Both SSI model configurations use Adam with initial learning rate 0.0002.
entries.condition: SSI spectral-regression experiment; Adam; applied to both model configurations.

entries.text: Frame-level training labels for the ultrasound CNN are generated by synchronizing speech frames to UTI frames and applying speech VAD.
entries.condition: Labels originate from the parallel synchronized audio; classifier input is one UTI frame.
entries.quote: We split the speech signal into frames and fed it to the speech VAD function to decide about the speech/silence label of each image.

entries.text: The 2D-CNN classifier uses binary cross-entropy and SGD with initial learning rate 0.001.
entries.condition: Frame-by-frame speech/silence classifier; binary cross-entropy loss.

entries.text: Speech labels outnumber silence labels by approximately 2–3 to 1.
entries.condition: Classifier training labels; labels come from the train, development, and test files.

entries.text: Table 3 configuration A reports MCD 1.55.
entries.condition: Speech-to-mel analysis and WaveGlow resynthesis; WebRTC VAD with 10 ms windows; dataset, speaker, and test split are not specified.
entries.quote: A: VAD (window length = 10 ms) 1.55

entries.text: Table 3 configuration B reports MCD 2.03 after retaining 180 ms of silence at both ends.
entries.condition: Speech-to-mel analysis and WaveGlow resynthesis; WebRTC VAD with 10 ms windows plus 180 ms silence at both ends; dataset, speaker, and test split are not specified.
entries.quote: B: VAD (window length = 10 ms), plus keeping 180ms silence at both ends 2.03

entries.text: Table 3 configuration C reports MCD 1.34 when configuration A is applied after B.
entries.condition: Speech-to-mel analysis and WaveGlow resynthesis; apply 10 ms-window VAD A after B; dataset, speaker, and test split are not specified.

entries.text: The authors conclude MCD is sensitive to the amount of silence in the input.
entries.condition: Based on silence-retention experiments and Fig. 3.
entries.quote: This result indicates that MCD is sensitive to the amount of silence in the input.

entries.text: The authors say WaveGlow does not reconstruct perfectly and is sensitive to silent duration and input-window positioning.
entries.condition: Explanation for the different MCD obtained by applying the analysis-synthesis configurations.

entries.text: The authors claim the BiLSTM model has a clear advantage over the 3D-CNN with a Dense layer, based on lower MSE and slightly lower MCD.
entries.condition: Comparison of the two SSI regressor architectures in Table 4; single-speaker TaL1; no significance test reported.

entries.text: 3D-CNN results are MSE(dev/test)/MCD 0.46/0.45/3.20 with silence removed and 0.30/0.33/3.29 with 180 ms retained.
entries.condition: TaL1, one male speaker; train/dev/test=1015/50/24 files; 3D-CNN; SSI input UTI and WaveGlow speech output; Adam LR 0.0002. MCD is described as test-set MCD. The two training conditions remove silence or retain 180 ms at both ends; seeds not stated.

entries.text: 3D-CNN+BiLSTM results are MSE(dev/test)/MCD 0.39/0.42/3.08 with silence removed and 0.259/0.29/3.13 with 180 ms retained.
entries.condition: TaL1, one male speaker; train/dev/test=1015/50/24 files; 3D-CNN+BiLSTM; SSI input UTI and WaveGlow speech output; Adam LR 0.0002. MCD is described as test-set MCD. The two training conditions remove silence or retain 180 ms at both ends; seeds not stated.

entries.text: The paper cites Ribeiro et al. as reporting MCD 2.99 on the same corpus with more sophisticated encoder-decoder networks.
entries.condition: Prior TaL-corpus SSI result attributed to Ribeiro et al. [20]; matched test split, speaker, and evaluation details are not supplied in this paper.

entries.text: The authors characterize their best MCD result as low-quality but intelligible speech.
entries.condition: Best reported SSI MCD is the 3D-CNN+BiLSTM, silence-removed result in Table 4.

entries.text: Retaining more silence lowers MSE, but the authors call this reduction misleading because test-set MCD rises slightly; they say the MCD increase is not significant.
entries.condition: Table 4 SSI training conditions; more silence is retained in the speech data while training the spectral regressor.

entries.text: Classifier accuracy is 0.87 on development and 0.852 on test.
entries.condition: Frame-level 2D-CNN on TaL1; dev=50 files and test=24 files from one male native speaker; labels from synchronized speech VAD; speech labels are approximately 2–3 times more frequent; decision threshold not reported; no independent speakers.
entries.quote: Accuracy 0.87 0.852

entries.text: Classifier recall is 0.94 on development and 0.95 on test.
entries.condition: Frame-level 2D-CNN on TaL1; dev=50 files and test=24 files from one male native speaker; labels from synchronized speech VAD; speech labels are approximately 2–3 times more frequent; positive-class mapping and decision threshold are not stated.
entries.quote: recall 0.94 0.95

entries.condition: Frame-level 2D-CNN on TaL1; dev=50 files and test=24 files from one male native speaker; labels from synchronized speech VAD; speech labels are approximately 2–3 times more frequent; positive-class mapping and decision threshold are not stated.

entries.condition: Frame-level 2D-CNN on TaL1; dev=50 files and test=24 files from one male native speaker; labels from synchronized speech VAD; speech labels are approximately 2–3 times more frequent; decision threshold was not tuned.

entries.condition: Frame-level 2D-CNN on TaL1; dev=50 files and test=24 files from one male native speaker; labels from synchronized speech VAD; speech labels are approximately 2–3 times more frequent.

entries.condition: TaL1, one male speaker; train/dev/test=1015/50/24 files; 3D-CNN SSI regressor; ultrasound-based VAD used to remove silence or retain 180 ms at both ends; Adam LR 0.0002; MCD described as test-set MCD; seeds not stated.

entries.text: The authors conclude ultrasound-based VAD performed similarly to speech-based WebRTC VAD in the SSI experiment.
entries.condition: Comparison in Table 7; single-speaker TaL1; the paper reports no statistical test of equivalence.
entries.quote:
In summary, we can say that our ultrasound-
based VAD algorithm performed similarly to the standard, speech-based VAD
algorithm in this experiment.

entries.text: The authors state the slight advantage of removing long silent parts remained when UTI-VAD replaced speech VAD.
entries.condition: SSI comparison in Table 7; effect is described qualitatively and no significance test is reported.

entries.text: The abstract reports approximately 85% speech/silence classification accuracy.
entries.condition: Headline result for the ultrasound-based speech/silence separator; detailed Table 5 test result is 0.852 on TaL1 test files.

entries.text: The abstract reports an AUC score around 0.86 for the ultrasound-based speech/silence separator.
entries.condition: Headline result; detailed Table 5 test ROC AUC is 0.859 on TaL1 test files.

entries.text: The conclusion rounds the classifier accuracy to 86%.
entries.condition: Conclusion headline; same speech/silence classifier evaluated on the single-speaker TaL1 test set.

entries.text: The authors propose using their VAD as an initial silence-removal step before feature extraction in future work.
entries.condition: Future plan: synchronize speech windows to ultrasound frames and retain only frames kept by VAD for synthesis or related tasks.

entries.text: The introduction suggests VAD may reduce energy consumption in wearable SSI devices; the paper does not evaluate that deployment benefit.
entries.condition: Motivation for SSI VAD, not an energy or device experiment.
entries.quote:
Similar to speech applications, voice activity detection may also be useful in
SSI systems, for example for sparing with the energy consumption in wearable
SSI devices.

entries.text: For the first speech-to-mel-to-WaveGlow experiment, the paper does not identify the dataset, speakers, or a test/validation split.
entries.condition: Table 3 analysis-synthesis MCD experiment; only the signal conversion and VAD configurations are described.

entries.text: The paper does not specify whether non-speech frames are excluded from its own MCD calculations or give the exact frame-alignment/scoring procedure.
entries.condition: Applies to the reported MCD experiments; the discussion notes that MCD silence handling is often unreported.

entries.text: Beyond the 10 ms window used in Table 3, the exact WebRTC VAD version and its mode/aggressiveness settings are not specified.
entries.condition: Speech VAD is used for silence removal and for generating classifier labels; no implementation version or remaining VAD parameters are reported.
entries.quote:
For voice activiry detection and silence removal we used the
VAD implementation available from WebRTC [26].

entries.text: No random seeds, independent-run count, or run-to-run variability are reported for the neural-network results.
entries.condition: SSI regressors and 2D-CNN classifier; the described repetitions change silence-removal conditions rather than specify repeated random-seed runs.

entries.text: Although 50 validation files are listed, the paper does not say how validation data selected hyperparameters, checkpoints, stopping points, or decision settings.
entries.condition: SSI and classifier experiments; validation/development data are reported, but their model-selection role is not described.

entries.text: The paper gives file counts but does not state whether files are separated by recording session or whether sessions overlap across splits.

We partitioned his ﬁles into training, testing and validation sets using
1015, 24 and 50 ﬁles, respectively.

entries.condition: All reported experiments use TaL1 from one male native speaker, so the paper does not test generalization to unseen speakers.

Similar to speech applications, voice activity detection may also be useful in

entries.text: The SSI mel-spectrogram target features use mean-deviance standardization, selected after the authors tried other normalization techniques.
entries.condition: SSI regression target features; 80 mel-spectrogram coefficients.

entries.text: The authors explain the lower MSE with retained silence by saying silence is easier to estimate than varied speech spectra.
entries.condition: SSI spectral-regression experiment with more silent samples retained in the training corpus.

entries.text: The authors say replacing speech VAD with UTI-VAD yielded slightly better MSE rates; the Table 7 values vary by model and dev/test split.

entries.quote: As the results in Table 7 show, in this case we obtained even slightly better MSE rates than earlier with the standard VAD function.

entries.text: Two-stage mapping: an ultrasound autoencoder compresses each image into bottleneck activations, then a second DNN predicts MGC-LSP spectral parameters and gain for vocoder synthesis.
entries.condition: Original F0 from the input speech was retained for synthesis; spectral parameters were predicted from ultrasound.

entries.text: Best reported autoencoder-based test-set spectral-parameter error: average NMSE for N=256 and 13 total ultrasound frames (six neighboring frames on each side).
entries.condition: Held-out test set: 87 utterances; one 42-year-old Hungarian female speaker; N=256, 13 frames; original F0 used for vocoder synthesis; no LM/decoding or seed reported.

entries.text: Average Pearson correlation on the test set for the same best-performing configuration (N=256, 13 total frames).

questions.q: Do the reported results establish that ultrasound VAD generalizes to unseen speakers?
questions.answer: No. All reported experiments use files from one male TaL1 speaker; no speaker-independent test is reported.

questions.q: Does the paper establish that UTI-VAD is equivalent to speech-based VAD?
questions.answer: It reports similar SSI metrics in one single-speaker experiment, but provides no equivalence test, uncertainty estimates, or independent runs.
